<section id="overview" class="content-section">

## What is Alignment?

**Alignment is the coordination of your base, posture, and limb positions so your body can support and direct force.**

When a movement fails, check your support points, torso position, and limb connection before adding effort. Recheck them whenever grips or pressure change.

</section>

<section id="building-blocks" class="content-section">

## Building Blocks
- Identify whether base, posture, or limb structure is failing.
- Keep working limbs connected to your torso.
- Support force from the direction it actually arrives.
- Disrupt their alignment before committing to a large movement.


</section>

<section id="prerequisites" class="content-section">

## Prerequisites
**Base diagnosis**: Locate your load-bearing points and test whether they can accept force from the direction it is actually arriving, not the direction you anticipated when you settled.

**Postural reading**: Check that head, spine, and pelvis are organized for the movement you intend, and notice early when your head has committed ahead of your hips.

**Structural connection**: Keep elbows, knees, and grips connected to the torso so no limb can be isolated by a local force smaller than your whole body could answer.

**Comparative assessment**: Read both players' alignment at once and decide whose is worse and in which direction, so you attack the broken element rather than the obvious one.

**Sequenced breaking**: Strip one element of the opponent's alignment - usually posture - and only then demand the large movement the position or pass requires.

**Recovery under load**: Restore one support at a time while preserving the others, choosing the cheapest missing piece first instead of fighting for the whole position at once.



</section>

<section id="where-to-apply" class="content-section">

## Where to Apply
**Clinch**: Keep your head supported over your hips while moving the opponent beyond a usable support point.

**Closed Guard**: Break the passer’s posture while keeping your own elbows and knees connected.

**Butterfly Guard**: Load weight onto your hooks while keeping your chest connected to the opponent.

**Knee Shield Half Guard**: Keep the shield connected to your hip so it supports space between your torsos.



</section>

<section id="how-to-apply" class="content-section">

## How to Apply
1. **What am I actually trying to do from here - advance, hold, or recover?**: Name the objective first, so that alignment is assessed against the movement you need rather than against how the position is supposed to look.
2. **Which of my own three elements is weakest right now?**: Test base, posture, and structure separately: can my support points take the incoming force, is my spine organized for the intended direction, is any limb working away from my torso?
3. **Which of the opponent's three elements is easiest to break?**: Pick the cheapest target - usually posture, then a support point - and decide the direction the break will travel before touching it.
4. **Can I act without giving up an element I still hold?**: If the action costs a support you currently own, rebuild first; if it only costs effort, commit and take the break.
5. **Did the break land, and what did the opponent spend to answer it?**: Read the answer: a structural reply means find another element, a muscular reply means the break landed and the large movement is now available.
6. **Has the exchange moved my alignment since I last checked?**: Re-read the three elements after every grip change, angle change, and weight shift, since the state moves even when the position name does not.
7. **Am I adding effort to cover a missing support?**: Stop, restore the missing element, and only then re-apply force - compensating with strength buys seconds and costs the round.
8. **Is the new position stable enough to leave?**: Confirm base under load and limbs reconnected before starting the next advance, so the following transition does not begin from a deficit.


</section>

<section id="mistakes-to-avoid" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## Mistakes to Avoid
- **Mistake**: Holding a rigid shape
  - **Consequence**: A useful position stops working when the force changes direction.
  - **Correction**: Adjust the relationship between support points, torso, and limbs.
- **Mistake**: Reaching beyond your base
  - **Consequence**: The grip leaves your body easy to pull or tip.
  - **Correction**: Move your support points with the reach.
- **Mistake**: Repairing only one part
  - **Consequence**: A wide base still fails with broken posture or an isolated arm.
  - **Correction**: Check base, posture, and structure together.


</section>

<section id="how-to-practice" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## How to Practice
**Freeze and diagnose** (Focus: Find the missing support.)
Roll cooperatively and pause on a signal. Each player names their base, posture, and limb structure, then identifies one adjustment before restarting.

**Transition checkpoints** (Focus: Keep alignment during movement.)
Walk through a familiar pass or sweep slowly. Pause when either player loses alignment, rewind that movement, and repeat with one adjustment.



</section>

<section id="progress-markers" class="content-section">

## Progress Markers
**Beginner Level**:
- Names base, posture, and structure separately in a paused exchange
- Notices when an arm has left the torso and brings the elbow back in
- Recognizes that control has been lost and resets rather than straining
- Demonstrates the principle with a cooperative partner in one or two positions


**Intermediate Level**:
- Breaks the opponent's posture before committing to a sweep or a pass
- Recovers one support at a time under light to moderate resistance
- Explains both the attacking and the defending side of the same exchange
- Stops adding effort when the cause is a missing support rather than insufficient force


**Advanced Level**:
- Holds usable alignment through changing positions rather than only in static shapes
- Picks the cheapest element to attack when the first route is blocked
- Re-reads alignment on grip and angle changes without prompting
- Combines alignment breaks with timing and angle to make the movement nearly free


**Expert Level**:
- Diagnoses subtle alignment failures under varied resistance and body types
- Chooses deliberately when to release a connection to gain a better one
- Attacks a specific element to provoke a predictable structural answer
- Teaches the principle from both roles using examples across unrelated positions




</section>

<section id="related" class="content-section">

## Related

### Related Principles
- **[[Base]]** (Prerequisite): Base is the support-point half of alignment; without load-bearing contacts that accept force, no posture or frame survives contact.
- **[[Posture]]** (Prerequisite): Posture is the spinal half of alignment and the element that usually breaks first, which is why most attacking sequences strip it before anything else.
- **[[Structure]]** (Complementary): Structure governs how limbs connect to the torso; aligned base and posture still lose a limb that is working away from the body.
- **[[Frames]]** (Complementary): Frames are the practical tool for holding structure under load, transmitting force through bone into the hips rather than into muscular effort.
- **[[Kuzushi]]** (Extension): Kuzushi is alignment disruption applied to the standing game - move the opponent past a usable support point before committing to the entry.
- **[[Center of Gravity]]** (Complementary): Where the mass sits relative to the support points determines whether a given alignment is stable or merely looks organized.
- **[[Connection Principles]]** (Complementary): Connection decides whether your alignment and the opponent's are coupled, so that breaking theirs feeds directly into your own movement.
- **[[Inside Position]]** (Complementary): Inside position supplies the leverage to attack alignment cheaply; from outside, the same break costs several times the effort.


### Related Content
- [[Positions/Closed Guard|Closed Guard]] (Position) - The classic posture-first laboratory: nearly every guard attack begins by breaking the passer's alignment.
- [[Positions/Mount|Mount]] (Position) - Top alignment decides whether weight is deliverable; bottom recovery is alignment repair before movement.
- [[Positions/Half Guard/Knee Shield Half Guard|Knee Shield Half Guard]] (Position) - A structural spacer held or flattened - the position is an argument about limb-to-torso connection.
- [[Positions/Back Control|Back Control]] (Position) - The defender's entire survival game is posture and chin-line alignment against the attacker's break.
- [[Positions/Ashi Garami|Ashi Garami]] (Position) - Leg entanglement is structural isolation applied to the leg, defended by reconnecting knee and hip.
- [[Positions/Headquarters Position|Headquarters Position]] (Position) - Passing stability here depends on a head that stays above the passer's own support line.
- [[Transitions/Body Lock Pass|Body Lock Pass]] (Transition) - A pass that works by removing the guard player's ability to organize hips and spine independently.
- [[Transitions/Back Step Pass|Back Step Pass]] (Transition) - Requires the passer to re-establish base and posture mid-rotation or hand back the guard.
- [[Submissions/Armbar|Armbar]] (Submission) - The canonical structural failure: a limb separated from the torso and then extended past its line.
- [[Principles/Base|Base]] (Principle) - The support-point element of alignment.
- [[Principles/Posture|Posture]] (Principle) - The spinal element of alignment, and usually the first one broken.
- [[Principles/Structure|Structure]] (Principle) - The limb-connection element of alignment.
- [[Principles/Frames|Frames]] (Principle) - The practical tool for holding structure under load.
- [[Principles/Kuzushi|Kuzushi]] (Principle) - Alignment disruption applied to the standing exchange.
- [[Systems/Gordon Ryan Passing System|Gordon Ryan Passing System]] (System) - A passing framework built on removing the guard player's alignment before advancing position.
